items.title: Clocks — angle formula and hand-position events
items.body:
### Angle between the hour and minute hands

**The idea in one sentence**
The two hands move at different speeds, so the gap between them changes every minute; to find the angle you work out how far each hand has travelled from the top of the clock (the 12) and subtract.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: what is the angle at 3:40?
1. The minute hand moves all the way round (360 degrees) in 60 minutes, so it moves 6 degrees every minute. At 40 minutes it is at 40 × 6 = 240 degrees from the 12.
2. The hour hand moves 360 degrees in 12 hours, which is 30 degrees per hour, or 0.5 degrees per minute. At 3:40 it has done 3 hours and 40 minutes, so 3 × 30 + 40 × 0.5 = 90 + 20 = 110 degrees from the 12.
3. The gap between them is 240 − 110 = 130 degrees. That is below 180, so the answer is 130 degrees.

**Why do we subtract from 360 sometimes?**
A clock is a circle, so two hands always make two angles that add up to 360. We quote the smaller one, so if the subtraction gives more than 180, take 360 minus that value.

**What the symbols mean**
Here H means the hour and M means the minutes past that hour. The number 5.5 means the minute hand gains 5.5 degrees on the hour hand every minute (6 minus 0.5), so one single number captures the whole race between the hands.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Angle = the size of (30 × H − 5.5 × M) degrees. If the result is above 180, subtract it from 360. The formula is just steps 1 and 2 above written in one line.

**Exam-level example**
At 5:30: 30 × 5 − 5.5 × 30 = 150 − 165 = −15; its size is 15 degrees. Check the slow way: minute hand at 180, hour hand at 5 × 30 + 15 = 165, gap 15 degrees. Correct.

**Common traps**
- Forgetting the hour hand keeps creeping forward during the minutes (using 150 for 5:00 at 5:30) gives a wrong 30 degrees.
- Leaving a negative sign in; always take the size (ignore the minus).
- Quoting an angle above 180 instead of subtracting from 360.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| minute hand = 6M | 6 degrees for every minute |
| hour hand = 30H + 0.5M | 30 per hour plus a little each minute |
| size of (30H − 5.5M) | the gap between the two hands |

### Times when the two hands meet, oppose or square up

**The idea in one sentence**
The minute hand chases the hour hand and gains a fixed amount every minute, so you can work out exactly when it catches up (0 degrees apart), when it is dead opposite (180 degrees apart) and when it is at a right angle (90 degrees apart).

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: between 4 and 5 o'clock, when do the hands overlap?
1. At 4:00 the hour hand is at the 4, which is 4 × 30 = 120 degrees from the 12. The minute hand is at the 12, so the minute hand is 120 degrees behind.
2. The minute hand gains 5.5 degrees every minute, so to wipe out a 120-degree gap it needs 120 ÷ 5.5 minutes.
3. 120 ÷ 5.5 = 240/11 = 21 and 9/11 minutes. So the hands overlap at about 4:21 and 9/11 of a minute.

**Why only 11 overlaps in 12 hours, not 12?**
You might expect one overlap each hour, so 12. But the hands move so that between 11 o'clock and 1 o'clock they only meet once (near 12:00), not twice. That removes one meeting, leaving 11 in every 12 hours.

**What the symbols mean**
"Coincide" means the two hands sit on top of each other (0 degrees). "Opposite" means they point exactly away from each other (180 degrees). 720/11 means 720 divided by 11, which works out to 65 and 5/11 minutes — the time between one overlap and the next.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Overlap minutes past hour H = 60H ÷ 11. For 90 or 180 degrees, set the size of (30H − 5.5M) equal to 90 or 180 and solve for M. In 12 hours: coincide 11 times, oppose 11 times, right angles 22 times.

**Exam-level example**
Between 2 and 3 o'clock, when are the hands first at a right angle? Set the size of (30 × 2 − 5.5M) = 90, so 5.5M − 60 = 90, giving M = 150 ÷ 5.5 = 300/11 = 27 and 3/11. So 2:27 and 3/11. Check: hour hand at 60 + 13.6 = 73.6, minute hand at 163.6, gap 90 degrees. Correct.

**Common traps**
- Counting 12 overlaps in 12 hours instead of 11.
- Forgetting the right-angle equation has two answers each hour (90 and −90).
- Using the minute number as the gap without turning it into degrees first.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| 60H ÷ 11 | minute past the hour when hands overlap |
| 720/11 = 65 5/11 min | time from one overlap to the next |
| 11, 11, 22 per 12 h | overlaps, opposites, right angles |
keyPoints: Angle between the hands = the size of (30H − 5.5M) degrees; if above 180, subtract from 360.
Minute hand moves 6 degrees per minute; hour hand 0.5 degrees per minute (gaining 5.5 per minute).
At 3:40 the angle is 130 degrees; at 5:30 it is 15 degrees.
Hands overlap at 60H ÷ 11 minutes past hour H, repeating every 65 and 5/11 minutes.
In 12 hours: coincide 11 times, oppose 11 times, right angles 22 times (double for 24 hours).
items.mnemonic: Thirty-times-the-hour minus five-and-a-half-times-the-minutes — the 5.5 is the minute hand's catch-up each minute.

items.title: Clocks — faulty clocks and mirror images
items.body:
### Faulty clocks and mirror images

**The idea in one sentence**
A faulty clock gains or loses a fixed amount every hour, so the total error just grows steadily with time; a mirror image flips the clock face left-to-right, so you measure the time backwards from 12 o'clock.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: a watch loses 3 minutes every hour and is set right at 6:00 a.m.; what true time does it show at 6:00 a.m. the next day?
1. From 6:00 a.m. to 6:00 a.m. is 24 hours.
2. It loses 3 minutes each hour, so in 24 hours it loses 3 × 24 = 72 minutes.
3. 72 minutes is 1 hour and 12 minutes. A losing watch runs behind, so it shows 6:00 a.m. minus 1 hour 12 minutes = 4:48 a.m.

**Why does a mirror use 12 o'clock as the fixed point?**
In a mirror the left and right swap, but 12 and 6 stay on the vertical line. So every position is measured as "how far before 12" instead of "how far after 12", which is the same as subtracting the time from 12:00.

**What the symbols mean**
"Gains" means the clock runs fast and shows a later time; "loses" means it runs slow and shows an earlier time. "11:60" means 12:00 written so you can subtract minutes without borrowing (60 minutes is one full hour).

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Total error = error per hour × hours elapsed. Mirror time = 12:00 − actual time, written as 11:60 − time when the minutes are not zero. Water image uses the 6:00 line instead of the 12:00 line.

**Exam-level example**
A clock gains 5 minutes an hour and is set right at 8:00 a.m. What does it show when the true time is 8:00 p.m.? From 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. is 12 hours, so it gains 5 × 12 = 60 minutes = 1 hour. A gaining clock runs ahead, so it shows 9:00 p.m. Check: 12 true hours, one extra hour added, 9:00 p.m. Correct.

**Common traps**
- Adding the error for a losing clock, or subtracting it for a gaining clock — losing runs behind, gaining runs ahead.
- Mixing up mirror image (fixed point 12:00) with water image (fixed point 6:00).
- Forgetting to carry when the minutes go below zero (use 11:60).

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| error per hour × hours | total minutes gained or lost |
| 11:60 − time | mirror image of a clock time |
| 3:25 to 8:35 | the mirror image of 3:25 |
keyPoints: Total error = error per hour × hours elapsed.
A losing clock shows an earlier time; a gaining clock shows a later time.
Mirror image of a time = 12:00 − time (use 11:60 − time when the minutes are not zero).
Mirror example: 3:25 becomes 8:35.
Water image uses the 6:00 reference line, which is different from the mirror's 12:00 line.
items.mnemonic: Lose means late becomes early; gain means it jumps ahead.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Clock

items.title: Calendars — odd days and finding the day of the week
items.body:
### Odd days and the day of the week

**The idea in one sentence**
Weekdays repeat every 7 days, so to find the day of any date you only need the days left over after taking out whole weeks — those leftovers are called "odd days".

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: how many odd days are in 200 years?
1. One ordinary year has 365 days. 365 = 52 weeks and 1 day left over, so an ordinary year has 1 odd day.
2. One leap year has 366 days, so 2 odd days.
3. In 100 years there are 76 ordinary years and 24 leap years (1900-type century rule), giving 76 × 1 + 24 × 2 = 124 days left over; 124 shared into weeks leaves 5 odd days. So 100 years give 5 odd days.
4. 200 years give 5 + 5 = 10 odd days; take out one whole week (7) to get 3 odd days.

**Why do we take out whole weeks?**
Seven days later is always the same weekday, so only the remainder after dividing by 7 changes the day. "63 mod 7" means the remainder when 63 is divided by 7, and that remainder is what moves the weekday.

**What the symbols mean**
"Odd days" means the leftover days after removing complete weeks. The month row below lists each month's odd days in an ordinary year; the word "mod 7" means divide by 7 and keep only the remainder.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Add the odd days from complete centuries, plus remaining years (count each leap year as 2), plus the month total, plus the date; take the result mod 7 and read off: 0 is Sunday, 1 Monday, up to 6 Saturday.

| Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 0 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 3 |

**Exam-level example**
What day was 15 August 1947? Adding 1600 years (0), 300 years (1), 46 completed years with their leap days, the month totals January to July and 15 days of August, the running total leaves 5 odd days from Sunday, which is Friday. A datetime check confirms 15 August 1947 was a Friday.

**Common traps**
- Counting a leap year as 1 odd day instead of 2.
- Using the leap-year month row (February 1) for an ordinary year.
- Forgetting the century rule when counting leap years inside 100 years.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| 365 to 1 odd day | an ordinary year moves the weekday by one |
| 100, 200, 300, 400 | 5, 3, 1, 0 odd days |
| total mod 7 | remainder gives the weekday |
keyPoints: Odd days are the leftover days after removing whole weeks; an ordinary year has 1, a leap year 2.
Century odd days: 100 give 5, 200 give 3, 300 give 1, 400 give 0.
Read the total mod 7 as 0 Sunday, 1 Monday, up to 6 Saturday.
Ordinary-year month odd days: 3, 0, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2, 3.
15 August 1947 was a Friday.
items.mnemonic: Century odd days count down in twos: five, three, one, zero.
items.source: local APPSC Logical Reasoning PDF — Calendar

items.title: Calendars — leap-year rule and calendar repetition
items.body:
### Leap years and when a calendar repeats

**The idea in one sentence**
A leap year adds an extra day (29 February) to keep the calendar in step with the seasons, and because that extra day shifts the weekdays, a whole calendar only repeats once the shifts cancel out to a full number of weeks.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: is 2000 a leap year but 1900 not?
1. The basic rule: a year divides evenly by 4 is a leap year. 2000 ÷ 4 = 500 and 1900 ÷ 4 = 475, so both look like leap years at first.
2. The exception: a century year (ending in 00) must also divide by 400. 2000 ÷ 400 = 5 exactly, so 2000 keeps its leap day.
3. 1900 ÷ 400 = 4.75, not whole, so 1900 loses its leap day and is an ordinary year. The same reasoning makes 2100 ordinary.

**Why does the same date jump forward each year?**
An ordinary year has 1 odd day, so the same date next year lands one weekday later. A leap year has 2 odd days, so the jump is two weekdays. That is why a date can skip a day.

**What the symbols mean**
"Divisible by 4" means 4 goes in with no remainder. "Leap status" means whether a year is leap or ordinary. The phrase "total odd days returns to a whole number of weeks" means the running leftover days add up to a multiple of 7.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Leap year = divisible by 4, but a century year must be divisible by 400. Same date next year moves 1 day (after an ordinary year) or 2 days (after a leap year). A calendar repeats when the odd days since that year total a multiple of 7 and the leap status matches.

**Exam-level example**
Which year repeats the 2023 calendar? 2023 is ordinary and starts on a Sunday. Adding odd days year by year, the first later year that both starts on a Sunday and is ordinary is 2034. A datetime check confirms 1 January 2023 and 1 January 2034 are both Sundays, so the calendars match.

**Common traps**
- Treating every year divisible by 4 as leap and forgetting the century exception.
- Matching only the start weekday but ignoring whether both years are leap or ordinary.
- Assuming the gap is always 11 years; ordinary years repeat after 6 or 11, leap years after 28.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| divisible by 4, century by 400 | the leap-year test |
| next year +1, after leap +2 | how the weekday jumps |
| 2023 repeats in 2034 | matching ordinary calendars |
keyPoints: Leap year: divisible by 4, but a century year must be divisible by 400.
2000 is a leap year; 1900 and 2100 are not.
The same date advances 1 day after an ordinary year and 2 days after a leap year.
A calendar repeats when the odd days total a multiple of 7 and the leap status matches.
Ordinary years repeat after 6 or 11 years; leap years after 28; 2023 repeats in 2034.
items.mnemonic: Divide by four, but a double-zero year must divide by four hundred.

items.title: Ages — ratio, difference and average methods
items.body:
### Solving age problems

**The idea in one sentence**
Every person ages by the same number of years at the same time, so you turn the words into one equation using parts for a ratio, a fixed difference, or a total, and then solve for the unknown.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: A and B are in the ratio 5 : 7 now; six years later they are 3 : 4; find their ages.
1. Write the present ages as 5 parts and 7 parts, so 5x and 7x, where x is the size of one part.
2. Six years later they are 5x + 6 and 7x + 6, and this is 3 : 4.
3. So 4 × (5x + 6) = 3 × (7x + 6), giving 20x + 24 = 21x + 18.
4. That leaves x = 6, so the ages are 5 × 6 = 30 and 7 × 6 = 42.

**Why add the time to both people?**
Six years pass for everyone at once, so both ages go up by 6. If you added it to only one person the difference between them would change, which never happens in real time.

**What the symbols mean**
"x" means the size of one ratio part. "N years hence" means N years in the future (add N to each age); "N years ago" means N years in the past (subtract N from each age). "Average" means the total divided by how many people there are.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Ratio: write parts kx, add or subtract the same time to each, set equal to the new ratio, solve. Difference stays fixed: if one is k years older, write A = B + k. New member's age = new average × (count + 1) − old average × count.

**Exam-level example**
Eleven players average 29 years; adding a coach raises the average to 30 across 12 people. Total of players = 11 × 29 = 319; total of twelve = 12 × 30 = 360; coach = 360 − 319 = 41. Shortcut check: coach = new average + rise × old count = 30 + 1 × 11 = 41. Both agree.

**Common traps**
- Adding the elapsed years to only one person.
- Reusing an old ratio later — ratios change as years pass, so re-solve each time.
- Mixing "ago" and "hence" signs; subtract for the past, add for the future.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| 5x, 7x | ratio parts for the two ages |
| A = B + k | one person is k years older for ever |
| new avg × (n+1) − old avg × n | the age of the person added |
keyPoints: For a ratio, write parts kx, add the same time to each age, set equal to the new ratio and solve.
The age difference stays constant; if one is k years older write A = B + k.
'N years ago' subtracts N from both ages; 'N years hence' adds N to both.
Added member's age = new average × (count + 1) − old average × count.
Ratios change as years pass, so always re-solve rather than reusing the old ratio.
items.mnemonic: Whatever years you give one age, give the other — they travel together.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Problem on Age / Based on Cricket and Age

items.title: Calendars — last day of a century and date shifts in a month
items.body:
### Last day of a century and date shifts within a month

**The idea in one sentence**
Because the calendar repeats exactly every 400 years, the last day of a century can only land on a few weekdays; and within one month two dates always differ by a whole number of days, so the weekday just shifts by that gap taken in weeks.

**Do it the slow way first (no formula)**
Question: if the 5th of a month is a Tuesday, what is the 21st?
1. The gap from the 5th to the 21st is 21 − 5 = 16 days.
2. Whole weeks do not change the weekday, so take out two weeks (14 days) from 16, leaving 2 days.
3. Move 2 weekdays on from Tuesday: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. So the 21st is a Thursday.

**Why can a century never end on certain days?**
Over 100, 200, 300 and 400 years the odd days are 5, 3, 1 and 0. Those four leftovers place the last day only on Friday, Wednesday, Monday or Sunday, so Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday are impossible.

**What the symbols mean**
"Odd days" means the leftover days after whole weeks. "16 mod 7" means the remainder when 16 is divided by 7, which is 2 — the number of weekdays you actually move. "Last day of a century" means 31 December of a year ending in 00.

**The formula (now that you know what it does)**
Within a month, weekday shift = (difference between the dates) mod 7. Last day of a century is only Sunday, Monday, Wednesday or Friday, using the century odd days 0, 1, 3 and 5.

**Exam-level example**
If 1 March is a Monday, what is 29 March? Gap = 28 days, which is exactly 4 weeks, so the remainder is 0 and the weekday does not move: 29 March is also a Monday. Check by listing: 1, 8, 15, 22, 29 March are all Mondays. Correct.

**Common traps**
- Taking the date number (21) mod 7 instead of the gap (16) mod 7.
- Thinking any weekday can be a century's last day.
- Forgetting that dates 7, 14, 21 or 28 apart share the same weekday.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| (date gap) mod 7 | how many weekdays to move |
| Sun, Mon, Wed, Fri | the only century last days |
| 7, 14, 21 apart | same weekday again |
keyPoints: The last day of a century is only Sunday, Monday, Wednesday or Friday — never Tuesday, Thursday or Saturday.
Century odd days: 100 give 5, 200 give 3, 300 give 1, 400 give 0.
Within a month the weekday shifts by (gap between the dates) mod 7.
If the 5th is a Tuesday, the 21st is a Thursday (gap 16, remainder 2).
Dates 7, 14, 21 or 28 days apart fall on the same weekday.
items.mnemonic: A century ends only on Sun, Mon, Wed or Fri.
